title: Lesson 14. Conditions
description: if / else, else if, && and ||, the ternary operator

learn.intro: Hi! Today we review **conditions** — lesson 14. I'll explain step by step, just like teacher {teacher} in class, and after each section we'll check what you remember. Let's go!

slides.text: The human brain makes decisions all the time: it's cold outside — I'll wear a jacket, it's not — I won't. JavaScript does the same thing with **conditions**.
Here's the pattern. Inside the parentheses `( )` we write a condition — its result is always `true` or `false`.
The code in curly braces runs only if the condition is true. And else means «otherwise»: it runs when the condition is false.
Example: can you buy a ticket for an 18+ movie. Here `age >= 18` is false, so the console shows «Sorry, this movie is 18+ only». Change age to 20 — and the message changes.

check.prompt: else runs when the condition is true.
check.explain: else means «otherwise». It runs when the condition is false.

check.prompt: What will the console show if age = 20?
check.explain: 20 >= 18 is true, so the if block runs.

sections.title: else if — a chain of conditions

slides.text: When there are more than two options, we add `else if` — «otherwise, if». For example, a grade by score:
JavaScript checks conditions **from top to bottom** and stops at the **first true one**. The rest are not checked. And `else` at the end means «in all other cases».
Order matters: write the strictest condition first (>= 90), then the softer one (>= 70). Swap them — and even 95 points will be «Good».

check.prompt: What does this code show when score = 40?
If score >= 70 is written first and score >= 90 second, 95 points will show «Excellent!».
check.explain: 95 >= 70 is already true, JavaScript stops checking and shows «Good».

slides.text: `&&` means **AND**: **both** conditions must be true. I'll go for a walk if the weather is good **AND** I have time.
The weather is good, but there's no time — so I stay home:
`||` means **OR**: **at least one** true is enough. I'll order pizza if I'm hungry **OR** just want it.
Remember this table — it's easy to check right in the console:
slides.code:
console.log(true && true);   // true
console.log(true && false);  // false
console.log(true || false);  // true
console.log(false || false); // false

check.explain: && needs both to be true. One false — and the whole result is false.
|| needs just one true — wantPizza = true.

slides.text: It's a **short if / else** in one line: `condition ? if_yes : if_no`.
Even or odd (remember `%` from lesson 13). Read it like this: «does the number divide by 2 with no remainder? If yes — “even”, if not — “odd”».
The ternary operator is for simple cases with two options. If there are more — write a normal if / else if.

check.prompt: What will the code show? Write the word.
check.explain: 15 >= 18 is false, so the value after the colon is taken.

check.prompt: The ternary operator is handy when there are 3 or more options.
check.explain: It's for two options. For three or more — if / else if.

sections.title: Practice: logging in to a site

slides.text: Let's put it all together. Here we have `else if`, `&&` and a template string:

In the homework you decide what to take from home using three variables: `temperature`, `isRaining`, `hasUmbrella`. You need at least 3 options and at least one condition with `&&` — for example, rain **and** no umbrella.

check.prompt: What does the login code show when age = 10?
check.explain: 10 < 12 — the very first condition is true, nothing else is checked.

questions.prompt: What goes in the parentheses ( ) after if?
questions.explain: Inside ( ) is the condition. Its result is always true or false.

questions.prompt: The code in curly braces { } after if runs only if the condition is true.
questions.explain: If the condition is false, this block is skipped and else runs (if there is one).

questions.prompt: Match the construct and its meaning
The expression true && false gives true.
questions.explain: && (AND) gives true only when both conditions are true. Here one is false — so the result is false.
|| (OR) gives true if at least one of the conditions is true.
75 >= 90 is false, 75 >= 70 is true. JavaScript stops at the first true condition.

questions.prompt: In an if / else if chain, JavaScript checks all conditions even after it finds a true one.
questions.explain: Conditions are checked from top to bottom, and checking stops at the first true one. The rest are not checked.
&& needs both conditions. hasTime = false, so the whole condition is false and else runs.

questions.prompt: What will the console show? Write the word.
questions.explain: 20 >= 18 is true, so the value after ? is taken, that is «adult».

questions.prompt: Build the ternary operator: if the number is even — «even», otherwise — «odd»
Match the operator and when it gives true
pairs: When at least one is true

questions.prompt: The conditions were swapped. What will the console show when score = 95?
questions.explain: 95 >= 70 is already true, and JavaScript checks no further. That's why the strictest condition (>= 90) goes first.
